question: The Council of the European Union formally adopted the revision of the EPBD1 on 12 April2. In 2023, the Commission criticised France in particular for its ‘lack of ambition regarding its long-term renovation strategy’, calling on it to gradually reform the Energy Performance Diagnosis (EPD) document for ‘harmonisation’ purposes3.

In December, the Commission stated that the revised rules provide for ‘[i]mproved EPCs4 [...] based on a common EU template with common criteria’5. However, the results of a study commissioned by the CEA6 on the energy performance of housing in France suggest that serious errors have been made.
Whilst the data does show that buildings with lower EPD ratings consume more energy, on average, this increase in energy consumption is six times lower than the EPD’s predicted figure7.

At a time when the EPBD is contributing to the highly concerning housing crisis in France by withdrawing between 500 000 and 800 000 homes from the rental market next year, is the Commission taking the conclusions of the CEA study seriously, and what lessons will it draw from these conclusions regarding its proposed EPCs with ‘common criteria’?

Energy Performance of Buildings Directive. ‘Contested EU green buildings law adopted’, Euractiv, 15 April 2024. ‘Petit tour d’Europe des diagnostics de performance énergétique’, Les actualités de BC2E, February 2024. Energy performance certificates.

‘The Commission welcomes the provisional agreement reached today between the European Parliament and the Council to reduce the emissions and energy use of buildings across the EU’, European Commission website, 7 December 2023. Council of Economic Analysis. ‘Performance énergétique du logement et consommation d’énergie: les enseignements des données bancaires’, Council of Economic Analysis website, 10 January 2024.
answer: As indicated in the Council of Economic Analysis (CEA) report, there are expected differences between estimated and actual energy consumption in buildings. The differences occur because the actual performance of a concrete building is significantly influenced by the behaviour of occupants or variations in local climate. It is necessary to account for these influences when comparing between buildings.

Therefore, these differences are a common occurrence. In order to develop national roadmaps for decarbonising and improving the EU building stock until 2050, the energy performance of buildings needs to be established. The Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) is an appropriate approach for this.
It is an asset rating tool based on a nationally standardised methodology, which allows for comparing and benchmarking between buildings.

The common criteria for EPC scales defined in the Energy Performance of Buildings Directive recast (EPBD) (8) leave ample flexibility to Member States to adapt their EPC schemes to reflect the performance and characteristics of their building stock and to differentiate at national and regional level.

Existing EPC schemes will be further strengthened through improvements in the calculation methodology and quality control. These elements will help to address some of the concerns raised in the CEA report. The Commission is currently working on guidance to support the Member States in the timely implementation of the EPBD recast.

The findings of the CEA study and results from other projects and initiatives will be taken into account. The recast of the EPBD does not oblige individual homeowners to renovate their buildings nor does it require to withdraw buildings from the rental market.
